name: Rigveda
info: The Rigveda is a collection of 1,028 Vedic Sanskrit hymns, composed most likely between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent. It is one of the four Vedas and is still recited in Hindu rites.

facts.made: Composed by poets of many clans, among them the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha; tradition ascribes each verse to a rishi, and the puranic tradition says Ved Vyasa compiled the Vedas
facts.form: Hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, in ten books (mandalas) with 1,028 hymns and about 10,600 verses, in metres such as the gayatri, anushtubh, trishtubh and jagati
facts.where: Read and recited in Hindu worship; thirty manuscripts at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007
facts.known: The oldest known Vedic Sanskrit text; hymns to Agni, Indra and Soma; the Gayatri Mantra (3.62.10); the Nasadiya Sukta, a hymn on the origin of the universe (10.129); the Purusha sukta; transmission by memory for centuries; a source for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European

t: The Rigveda is the oldest known Vedic Sanskrit text, a collection of 1,028 hymns in ten books, mostly to gods such as Agni, Indra and Soma, and most scholars place its bulk between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE.

Hindu tradition classes the Vedas as shruti, "what is heard"; scholars study the text as the work of human poets of many clans, and the Rigveda's own hymns name poets rather than claim a divine author.
It passed from teacher to pupil by memory with great fidelity, and its oldest surviving manuscripts, found in Nepal, date only to c. 1040 CE.
dyk: The Shatapatha Brahmana gives the number of syllables in the Rigveda as 432,000, while the metrical text of van Nooten and Holland (1994) counts 395,563.
ev: Most likely span of the composition of the bulk of the Rigveda Samhita in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent
Codification of the hymns into ten books by members of the early Kuru tribe, on Witzel's account
The fixing of the Vedic chant and of the padapatha, during the later Brahmana period
Yaska discusses the meanings of difficult words of the Rigveda in his Nirukta
Date of the oldest surviving manuscripts, found in Nepal
Sayana writes a commentary on the complete text
Max Müller publishes a six-volume translation into German
Thirty manuscripts at Pune are added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register

sections.origins:
The Rigveda Samhita is a collection of hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, an early Indo-Aryan language. Philological and linguistic evidence indicates that the bulk of it was composed in the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, most likely between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE, although a wider approximation of c. 1900–1200 BCE has also been given. Jamison and Brereton, in their 2014 translation, call the dating a matter of contention that is likely to remain so, since every proposal is inferred from the style and content of the hymns themselves. The hymns must post-date the Indo-Iranian separation, dated to roughly 2000 BCE, and the Mitanni documents of northern Syria and Iraq (c. 1450–1350 BCE), which mention Vedic gods such as Varuna, Mitra and Indra, offer a reasonable comparison for the date of the core.

The text shows strong linguistic and cultural similarities with the early Iranian Avesta, which derive from Proto-Indo-Iranian times and are often associated with the early Andronovo culture of c. 2000 BCE. According to Jamison and Brereton, the hymns give no evidence of an elaborate or structured caste system. The society they glimpse was semi-nomadic and pastoral, with some agriculture, since hymns mention the plough. Frits Staal counts about 300 words in the text that are neither Indo-Aryan nor Indo-European, and Michael Witzel takes them as a sign that its speakers already knew and interacted with Munda and Dravidian speakers.
sections.content:
The Rigveda Samhita is the core text. It has ten books, called mandalas ("circles"), with 1,028 hymns (sūktas) in about 10,600 verses (ṛc, from which the name Rigveda comes). The hymns praise many deities. Chief among them are Indra, a heroic god praised for slaying his enemy Vrtra, Agni, the sacrificial fire, and Soma, the sacred potion or the plant it is made from. Mitra and Varuna, Ushas (the dawn), Vishnu, Rudra and natural forces such as the wind and the waters are also invoked. Hymn 1.1 is addressed to Agni, and his name is the first word of the text. The ninth mandala is devoted entirely to Soma.

Books 2 to 9, the earliest, deal mostly with cosmology and with the rites that win the favour of the gods. Books 1 and 10, the youngest, also take up philosophical questions, charity, and the origin of the universe. The tenth book holds the Nasadiya Sukta (10.129), which sets out several speculations about creation and asks whether anyone can know the right answer, and the Purusha sukta, which has been important in studies of Vedic sociology. Verse 3.62.10 is the Gayatri Mantra, of great importance in Hinduism. In the wider sense the name Rigveda also covers the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads handed down with the Samhita.
sections.making:
The "family books" (2 to 7) are tied to particular clans and chieftains, each book holding hymns by members of one clan, and they mention prominent Bharata and Pūru kings. Tradition associates a rishi (the composer) with each verse, and ten families of rishis account for more than 95 per cent of the verses. Books 1, 8 and 10 look like collections of verses in different styles, which suggests many authors. Book 10 appears from its language to have been composed and added last.

According to Witzel, the hymns were codified at the end of the Rigvedic period, c. 1200 to 1000 BCE, in the early Kuru kingdom, after the Bharata victory under king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings; the collection was an effort to reconcile factions among the clans. Asko Parpola likewise argues that the text was systematised around 1000 BCE. The family books are ordered by deity, then by the number of stanzas, then by metre. A later redaction, contemporary with that of the other Vedas, added some hymns and regularised the sandhi (the joining of sounds between words). The fixing of the chant and of the padapatha, which divides the text word by word, belongs to roughly the 6th century BCE.
sections.reception:
The Vedas are classed in Hindu tradition as shruti, which has been compared to divine revelation in Western religious thought. Staal argues that the Rigveda nowhere states that it was revealed. For him shruti means simply what is heard, passed from teacher to pupil, and the reverential term apauruṣeya (not of human origin) appears only centuries after the Vedic period, in the Mimamsa school. The text itself suggests, he says, that it was composed by human poets whose names were household words. In the Puranic tradition, Ved Vyasa compiled the four Vedas and taught the Rigveda to Paila; an alternative version says Shakala compiled it from the teachings of the rishis.

Yaska (4th century BCE) was an early commentator, and in his Nirukta he holds that the text can be read in three ways: by rite, by deity and by the soul. By the medieval period the language had become almost unintelligible, and interpretation leaned on mystical ideas. Sāyana wrote a commentary on the whole text in the 14th century, and Madhvacharya one on the first 40 hymns in the 13th. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, Dayananda Saraswati, who in Robson's account held that the Vedas contained no errors, and Sri Aurobindo, who thought Sayana too ritualistic, read the hymns as monotheistic or mystical. Axel Michaels and Louis Renou describe the reverence of most Indians today as slight.
sections.survival:
For more than a millennium the fixed text was preserved by oral tradition alone, through a very structured enunciation that broke Sanskrit compounds into stems and inflections. The padapatha isolates each word, while the samhitapatha, joined by sandhi, is the form recited. This gave rise to a scholarly tradition of morphology and phonetics. It is unclear when the Rigveda was first written down. Barbara West thinks probably in the 3rd century BCE, while Witzel points to written manuscripts c. 800–1000 CE and notes that Smriti rules forbade writing down the Vedas. The oral tradition continued into modern times. The oldest surviving manuscripts were found in Nepal and date to c. 1040 CE. Birch bark and palm leaf decay, so the text was copied over the generations.

Several recensions (shakhas) existed, but only the Śākala survives in full; the Bāṣkala may also survive, though this is uncertain. The Śākala has 1,017 regular hymns and 11 vālakhilya hymns, 1,028 in all. In Aufrecht's 1877 edition the hymns hold 10,552 verses. Thirty manuscripts at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, in the Sharada and Devanagari scripts, were collected in the 19th century; the oldest of them dates to 1464 CE, and they joined UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007. Manuscripts have also been found in Grantha, Malayalam and Nandinagari scripts.
sections.legacy:
The Rigveda is far more archaic than any other Indo-Aryan text, which made it a centre of Western scholarship from the time of Max Müller and Rudolf Roth. Its preserved archaic syntax and morphology matter for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European, and its hymns resemble the Gathas of old Avestan and Homer's Iliad. Rosen made the first published translation of a portion, into Latin. Müller published a six-volume German translation in 1849, and H. H. Wilson published the first English one from 1850 to 1888. Geldner completed the first scholarly German translation in the 1920s, and van Nooten and Holland restored the whole text to its poetic form in 1994. Staal calls the text obscure and difficult, and warns that it has often been misinterpreted.

Some verses are still recited at weddings and other rites of passage, which makes it probably the world's oldest religious text in continued use. The marriage hymns (10.85) and death hymns (10.10 to 18) remain important in household rituals, and Rigvedic hymns appear in Carnatic compositions such as Hamsadhvani. The text also figures in modern debates over Indian identity. Bal Gangadhar Tilak argued in 1893 for a composition date of at least 6000–4000 BCE, and "Out of India" arguments link it with the Indus Valley civilisation; mainstream scholarship does not accept these theories.

summary: The Rigveda is the oldest known Vedic Sanskrit text, a collection of 1,028 hymns in ten books composed most likely between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE. Handed down orally for centuries, it is a Hindu shruti text and an important source for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European.
